title: Renewable Deployment
summary:
Renewables have won on cost — onshore wind and solar PV are now the cheapest new generation in most of the world — so the deployment story is no longer 'is it cheap enough?' but **'how do we build it fast, finance it, and fit it into the grid?'** Understanding that shift is the core of an energy analyst's job.

The headline metric is **LCOE (levelized cost of energy)**: the lifetime cost of a project divided by its lifetime output, both discounted, giving a single €/MWh figure to compare technologies. LCOE is powerful but treacherous — it hides *when* and *where* the energy is produced. A solar farm and a gas plant with the same LCOE are not equivalent: one generates only when the sun shines. So analysts pair LCOE with the **capacity factor** (actual output ÷ theoretical maximum if it ran flat-out all year): ~10–25% for solar PV, ~25–45% for onshore wind, ~40–60% for offshore wind, vs ~90% for nuclear. Capacity factor is *not* efficiency — it is about availability and resource, not how well fuel is converted.

Because wind and solar are **variable** (they follow the weather, not demand), large penetrations create two problems. First, **curtailment**: when output exceeds what the grid can absorb or transmit, operators dump some of it — wasted, but increasingly common. Second, **price cannibalization**: every extra solar panel pushes down the price *during sunny hours* (the merit-order effect, seen in [[project-energy-companion]]'s pm01), so a solar farm's **capture price** — the average price it actually earns, weighted by its own output — falls below the market average. The **value factor** (capture price ÷ average price) drops as a technology scales. This is why pure merchant exposure gets riskier with penetration, and why revenue-stabilising contracts matter.

Those contracts are the financing backbone. A **feed-in tariff (FiT)** pays a fixed €/MWh — simple but expensive for governments. **Auctions / tenders** let developers compete to build for the lowest support level, driving costs down dramatically. A **Contract for Difference (CfD)** tops up (or claws back) the difference between a strike price and the market price, giving the developer revenue certainty while protecting consumers when prices are high. A corporate **PPA** does the same job privately. All exist because lenders finance renewables on *predictable* cash flows, and a subsidy-free merchant project facing cannibalised, volatile prices is hard to bank.

Finally, deployment is increasingly **grid- and permit-limited, not cost-limited**. Projects wait years in **interconnection queues**, **permitting/consenting** is the critical-path bottleneck, and **system-integration costs** (grids, balancing, firming) rise with penetration even as generation LCOE falls. The frontier is hybridisation — **co-locating** solar, wind and storage to firm output and lift the capture price — and siting flexible demand (including data centres, see gr01) where the renewable resource and grid capacity actually exist.

equations.name: Levelized cost of energy (LCOE)
equations.useWhen: Comparing the lifetime €/MWh cost of different technologies on a like-for-like basis. Use the simplified form for a quick back-of-envelope; the full form discounts costs $I_t,M_t,F_t$ (capex, O&M, fuel) and energy $E_t$ at rate $r$.
equations.note: LCOE ignores *when* (timing/capture price) and *where* (grid/integration cost) the energy is produced — never compare a variable and a dispatchable source on LCOE alone.

equations.name: Capacity factor
equations.useWhen: Turning a plant's nameplate MW into expected annual MWh, or sizing a project for a target output. 8760 = hours in a year.
equations.note: **Not efficiency.** CF measures how much of the year a plant effectively runs at full power (resource + availability), not how well it converts fuel.

equations.name: Value (capture) factor
equations.useWhen: Judging the *revenue* quality of a variable renewable, not just its cost. $\bar P_{capture}$ is the output-weighted average price the asset earns; a falling value factor signals cannibalization as the technology scales.
equations.note: VF < 1 for solar/wind (they earn below average because they all produce at the same times); VF can exceed 1 for dispatchable peakers.

glossary.definition: Lifetime discounted cost ÷ lifetime discounted output, in €/MWh. The standard cost-comparison metric — but blind to timing and location.
Actual annual output ÷ output if the plant ran at rated power all year. ~10–25% solar, ~25–45% onshore wind, ~40–60% offshore, ~90% nuclear. Not efficiency.
The fraction of a variable plant's nameplate that can be relied on at peak for adequacy. Low for solar at a winter-evening peak, hence the need for firm capacity.
Output set by weather, not demand. The defining challenge of wind and solar — it drives curtailment, balancing needs and cannibalization.
Deliberately reducing available renewable output when the grid can't absorb or transmit it. Rises with penetration and grid congestion; sometimes compensated.
The output-weighted average price a generator actually earns. For solar/wind it sits below the time-average market price because they all produce at once.
Capture price ÷ average market price. Falls below 1 and declines as a variable technology scales — the quantified form of cannibalization.
Each added solar/wind unit depresses the price in its own production hours (merit-order effect), eroding the revenue of all similar assets.
A two-way contract paying the gap between a strike price and the market price (and clawing back when prices are higher). Gives revenue certainty while protecting consumers.
A fixed guaranteed €/MWh for renewable output. Simple and effective for early deployment, but costly and not market-responsive — largely superseded by auctions/CfDs.
Competitive procurement where developers bid the lowest support level (€/MWh or capacity) to win the right to build. The main driver of recent cost falls.
A private long-term power-purchase contract (often a CfD-style hedge) that underwrites a project's revenue so it can be financed without state subsidy. (See pm01.)
A project relying on market (spot/PPA) revenue with no public support. Increasingly viable but exposed to cannibalized, volatile capture prices.
Whether a green purchase or PPA actually causes *new* renewable capacity to be built, rather than just re-labelling existing generation. Central to credible corporate claims.
Replacing ageing turbines (or panels) with larger, more efficient modern ones on an existing site — boosting output without new permits or land.
The backlog of projects waiting for permission and capacity to connect to the grid. Now a primary bottleneck — often a multi-year wait.
Securing planning, environmental and land permissions. Frequently the critical path for deployment, especially for onshore wind and grid lines.
Power (or energy) produced per unit land or sea area (W/m²). Solar and wind are far less dense than thermal plants, making siting and land a real constraint.
Offshore has higher, steadier wind (higher capacity factor) and bigger turbines, but higher capex and grid-connection cost; onshore is cheaper but more permit-constrained.
PV converts light directly to electricity (cheap, modular, no storage by itself); CSP concentrates heat to drive a turbine and can include thermal storage for dispatchability.
The extra grid, balancing and firming costs renewables impose on the system, beyond their own LCOE. Rises with penetration — why 'cheapest LCOE' isn't the whole story.
Combining variable generation with storage, demand response or other plants to deliver more predictable, schedulable ('firm') output.
Solar + wind + storage sharing one grid connection and site. Raises the capture price, smooths output and uses scarce connection capacity better.
The slow annual decline in a solar panel's (or battery's) output, typically ~0.5%/yr for PV — factored into lifetime energy and LCOE.
A policy mandate for a share of energy from renewables by a date (e.g. EU 2030 targets), creating the demand that auctions and CfDs deliver against.
Near-zero-marginal-cost renewables push the supply stack right, lowering wholesale prices — the mechanism behind cannibalization. (See pm01.)

tips: **Capacity factor ≠ efficiency.** A 20% solar CF doesn't mean 20%-efficient panels — it means the array averages 20% of its nameplate over the year. Use $CF\times P\times 8760$ to get annual MWh.
**LCOE compares cost, not value.** Two sources with equal LCOE differ hugely if one is dispatchable. Always pair LCOE with capacity factor and capture price before drawing conclusions.

**More solar lowers solar's own revenue.** Cannibalization means the capture price (and value factor) falls as penetration grows — the economic case shifts toward storage, hybridisation and flexible demand.
**Deployment is grid- and permit-limited now, not cost-limited.** Connection queues and consenting, not turbine prices, are the binding constraints — a key thing to flag in any deployment analysis.
**CfD vs PPA vs merchant = who carries price risk.** CfD (government), PPA (corporate offtaker), merchant (the developer). Financing follows whoever provides predictable cash flow.

**Curtailment is a feature of success.** Rising curtailment signals that generation has outpaced grid and flexibility — an argument for storage, interconnection and demand-side response, not for stopping deployment.
